summary: Specifies the telnet URI scheme, previously described in RFC 1738. It was written so that RFC 1738 could be made obsolete while the scheme's description stays on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC keeps the Telnet URI scheme defined separately from RFC 1738. The URI points to an interactive Telnet service, and the document warns that ordinary Telnet does not protect passwords or session contents.

subtitle: The URI scheme for identifying an interactive service that can be accessed with Telnet.

tldr.problem: The Telnet URI definition was part of RFC 1738, which was being obsoleted, so the scheme needed a separate standards-track description.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the telnet URI form with an optional user, password and port; the default port is 23.
tldr.outcome: The URI identifies an interactive service, not a data object. The RFC warns that ordinary Telnet exposes passwords and session contents without protection.

today: RFC 4248 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 1738 for the Telnet URI scheme. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Scheme Has a Separate RFC
sections.content:
RFC 1738 originally defined many URI schemes, including the Telnet scheme. Because RFC 1738 had become obsolete, RFC 4248 copies the Telnet scheme definition so that it can remain on the standards track.

The RFC also refers to the general URI syntax defined by RFC 3986.
sections.plainLanguage: The Telnet URI rules were part of an older document that was being retired. This RFC gives those rules their own document.

sections.title: The telnet URI Form
sections.content:
A telnet URI identifies an interactive service available through the Telnet protocol. Its form is telnet://<user>:<password>@<host>:<port>/. The final slash may be omitted, and the port defaults to 23 if it is not supplied.

The password may be omitted, as may the entire user and password part. Usernames and passwords in the URI are advisory: clients merely show the user the suggested values. The URI does not identify a data object.
sections.plainLanguage: The URI names a host and may include a user, password and port. If no port is given, it defaults to 23; login details in the URI are only suggestions.

sections.title: Security of Telnet Sessions
sections.content:
Ordinary Telnet normally sends passwords in the clear and provides no privacy. A user's identity, password and session contents can therefore be exposed. Some Telnet extensions provide ways to improve security, but the telnet URI does not require clients to use them.

Some clients try to use more secure Telnet options, while others do not. The RFC says users cannot rely on this security unless it is explicitly enabled and the result of the security negotiation is checked.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary Telnet does not protect passwords or session contents. A user must explicitly enable a security extension and check that negotiation succeeded before relying on it.
